title: 1 Chronicles 21:18–30
context: At the angel’s command, David buys Ornan’s threshing floor, builds an altar, and offers sacrifices, and the LORD answers with fire from the sky; the angel sheathes his sword. The Chronicler explains that the tabernacle and the altar were then at Gibeon, but David feared to go there. The parallel in 2 Samuel 24:18-25 gives fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and the oxen, while 21:25 gives six hundred shekels of gold for the place, and Samuel does not mention the fire on the altar. These differences are left as they stand.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s angel commanded Gad to tell David that David should go up and raise an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s angel commands Gad to tell David to raise an altar on Ornan’s threshing floor. Arminian readers see God himself providing the way for judgment to end, turning a place of threatened destruction into a place of worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the command comes through the angel to Gad and then to David, emphasizing that the place of worship is chosen by God, not by the king. Chronicles adds the angel’s role in giving the command.

verses.text: David went up at the saying of Gad, which he spoke in the LORD’s name.
verses.arminianNotes: David went up at the saying of Gad, spoken in the LORD’s name. Arminian readers see repentance moving into prompt obedience, the practical evidence that confession was more than words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David submits to God’s word through the prophet without delay. The phrase in the LORD’s name stresses that Gad’s instruction carried divine authority.

verses.text: Ornan turned back and saw the angel; and his four sons who were with him hid themselves. Now Ornan was threshing wheat.
verses.arminianNotes: Ornan turns, sees the angel, and his four sons hide while he is threshing wheat. Arminian readers note the fear that God’s holiness provokes even in a foreigner, and that this detail is absent from 2 Samuel 24.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Chronicles places Ornan at ordinary work when the angel appears. The sight of the angel, the hiding sons, and the threshing wheat are details found only in this account.

verses.text: As David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David, and went out of the threshing floor, and bowed himself to David with his face to the ground.
verses.arminianNotes: Ornan sees David, leaves the threshing floor, and bows with his face to the ground. Arminian readers see humility on both sides, as a king comes seeking mercy and a Jebusite receives him with honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the reversal: the king who ordered a census to measure his strength now comes in need to a foreigner’s field. The scene matches 2 Samuel 24:20 in Ornan’s reverent greeting.

verses.text: Then David said to Ornan, “Sell me the place of this threshing floor, that I may build an altar to the LORD on it. You shall sell it to me for the full price, that the plague may be stopped from afflicting the people.”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks to buy the place for the full price so the plague may be stopped. Arminian readers see David acting as intercessor for the people, seeking the end of their suffering through God’s appointed means.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David insists on paying the full price from the start, a phrase not found in 2 Samuel 24:21. The altar is built for the people’s sake, which both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: Ornan said to David, “Take it for yourself, and let my lord the king do that which is good in his eyes. Behold, I give the oxen for burnt offerings, and the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat for the meal offering. I give it all.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ornan offers the oxen, the threshing instruments, and the wheat for the meal offering, saying, I give it all. Arminian readers see generosity in a foreigner who honors Israel’s king and his God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Chronicles adds wheat for a grain offering to the gifts named in 2 Samuel 24:22. Ornan’s offer is gracious, but David will not accept it as a gift.

verses.text: King David said to Ornan, “No, but I will most certainly buy it for the full price. For I will not take that which is yours for the LORD, nor offer a burnt offering that costs me nothing.”
verses.arminianNotes: David refuses to offer a burnt offering that costs him nothing. Arminian readers see the principle that genuine worship involves personal cost, and they apply it to the way believers give themselves to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wholehearted devotion that will not offer God what belongs to another. Many Christians apply the principle to the living sacrifice of Romans 12:1, presented as an application rather than the verse’s direct sense.

verses.text: So David gave to Ornan six hundred shekels of gold by weight for the place.
verses.arminianNotes: David gives Ornan six hundred shekels of gold by weight for the place. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 24:24 says fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and the oxen, and they leave the difference unresolved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also name the difference between six hundred shekels of gold for the place and fifty shekels of silver in Samuel. Interpreters explain it in more than one way, and the notes here do not choose among them.

verses.text: David built an altar to the LORD there, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and called on the LORD; and he answered him from the sky by fire on the altar of burnt offering.
verses.arminianNotes: David builds an altar, offers sacrifices, calls on the LORD, and God answers from the sky by fire. Arminian readers see God’s gracious acceptance of the offering, a public sign that the way of mercy is open again.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the fire on the altar appears only in Chronicles; 2 Samuel 24:25 says the LORD was entreated and the plague removed. Fire from heaven recalls other moments when God accepted sacrifice (Leviticus 9:24; 1 Kings 18:38).

verses.text: Then the LORD commanded the angel, and he put his sword back into its sheath.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD commands the angel, and he sheathes his sword. Arminian readers see judgment ending in response to sacrifice and prayer, the merciful answer David had sought for his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign command ending what he had begun. The sheathed sword, found only in Chronicles, completes the image of the angel with the drawn sword in 21:16.

verses.text: At that time, when David saw that the LORD had answered him in the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, then he sacrificed there.
verses.arminianNotes: When David sees that the LORD answered him at Ornan’s threshing floor, he sacrifices there. Arminian readers see David continuing in worship once God has shown his acceptance, not merely stopping when the danger ends.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s answer marks the place as acceptable for sacrifice. The verse prepares for 22:1, where David declares this to be the site of the house of the LORD.

verses.text: For the LORD’s tabernacle, which Moses made in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offering, were at that time in the high place at Gibeon.
verses.arminianNotes: The tabernacle Moses made and the altar of burnt offering were then at the high place at Gibeon. Arminian readers see the Chronicler explaining why David sacrificed somewhere other than the established altar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this explanation, absent from Samuel, shows the Chronicler’s concern for proper worship. The verse acknowledges the Mosaic tabernacle while preparing for a new, permanent place.

verses.text: But David couldn’t go before it to inquire of God, for he was afraid because of the sword of the LORD’s angel.
verses.arminianNotes: David could not go to Gibeon to inquire of God because he feared the angel’s sword. Arminian readers see a sobered king who now takes God’s holiness with full seriousness after the census.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the angel’s sword keeping David at the place God had chosen. His fear becomes part of the way God fixes the site of future worship, which the next chapter makes explicit.
